analysis.one_liner: Cuts off all federal funding for carrying out the Affordable Care Act.
analysis.headline: The bill to strip funding from the Affordable Care Act was referred to six House committees, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would declare that no federal money may be appropriated to carry out the Affordable Care Act or the 2010 health-and-student-loan reconciliation law that amended it [S2][S3]. Because the health law's grants, prevention programs, and administrative work depend on yearly appropriated funding, cutting that off would hobble the law even without repealing it. It would not touch the health law's taxes or its insurance market rules, which are written into permanent law and do not depend on annual funding [S3]. The bill was referred to six committees in January 2011 and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the federal government would have spent less on implementing the health law, and opponents of the law would have advanced their goal of starving it without a repeal fight.

how_it_helps.text: Declares that no funds are authorized to be appropriated to carry out the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act, the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010, or any amendment made by either law [S2][S3].

Because the language applies 'notwithstanding any other provision of law,' it would override every existing funding authorization for those laws, stopping appropriations for the law's grant programs, prevention fund, and implementation work [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Uninsured and lower-income people who were beginning to get help from the law's coverage programs, communities receiving its prevention and public health grants, and the insurers, hospitals, and drug makers counting on newly insured customers under the law.
analysis.who_pays_short: People relying on the law's coverage help

drawbacks.text: The bill cuts funding without repealing the law. The health law's tax increases and insurance market rules stay in permanent law regardless of appropriations, so passage could leave people paying the law's taxes while its benefits are starved of operating money [S3].

It would defund all of the health law's appropriated programs in one stroke, including public health and prevention grants that communities use for local health programs, with no phase-out or replacement [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real federal savings in principle, but it was a blunt instrument: it would have cut off the money for benefits and programs that help people buy coverage and run local health programs, while leaving the law's taxes and mandates standing on their own. An honest supporter of cutting the law would acknowledge that deauthorization alone is a poor substitute for actual repeal, because it damages the law's operation without resolving anything about its design [S3].

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to six House committees the day it was introduced, a couple of subcommittees took referrals of pieces of it, and it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Tom Graves introduced the bill on January 5, 2011, the opening day of the 112th Congress, with ten original cosponsors [S1][S3].

It was referred to six committees at once — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, Judiciary, Natural Resources, and House Administration — a multi-committee referral that makes a bill harder to move [S5].

On January 26, 2011 a subcommittee took a referral of part of it, and on February 1, 2011 the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee got a referral; after that, the action history shows nothing further for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The bill accumulated 74 cosponsors, all Republicans [S4], but no committee ever reported it and the House never voted on it before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, Affordable Care Act funding continued as normal: the people gaining coverage help and prevention grants under the law kept them, and the insurers, hospitals, and drug makers whose new business the law created kept it too. Nobody had to change anything, because a bill with 75 Republican backers was never brought up for a decision.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The health law's beneficiaries and backers

for.name: Tom Graves
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 112th Congress and sought cosponsors to defund the health law [S1][S3].

against.name: House committee chairs
against.role: Chairs of the six committees of referral, including Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; the record shows no committee action after the early-2011 subcommittee referrals [S5].

against.name: John Boehner
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor, while House Republicans pursued a full repeal of the health law through a separate bill in January 2011.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 74 cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support, in a House where Republicans held the majority.

industries.note: The health law channels subsidies to people buying coverage through private insurers; cutting off funding for the law would end that subsidy pipeline, costing insurers millions of subsidized new customers. Ordinary people losing coverage help and insurers losing those customers lose together under this bill.

Providers counted on fewer uninsured patients as the law's coverage expanded; defunding would preserve uncompensated care burdens while also ending some public health and prevention funding streams that flow to community programs.

Drug makers gained newly insured customers under the law but accepted new rebate obligations in return; defunding the law would cost them customers while relieving them of some of those obligations, leaving the net effect uncertain.
